title: Galata Tower
excerpt: Global supply chains and geopolitical balances increasingly pivot around Galata Tower. Tracking the primary facts helps separate durable structural shifts.
author: Anne Hardy

body.text: Global supply chains and geopolitical balances increasingly pivot around Galata Tower. Tracking the primary facts helps separate durable structural shifts from daily noise.

Galata Tower (Turkish: Galata Kulesi), or Galata Tower Museum (Turkish: Galata Kulesi Müzesi), its name since it began to be used as a museum, is a tower located in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul. It takes its name from the Galata neighborhood where it stands.

Built as a watchtower within the Walls of Galata, the tower has served various purposes over different periods and has functioned as an exhibition venue and museum since 2020. It is one of the landmark structures of both Beyoğlu and Istanbul.

In 1267, the Genoese, who were allied with the Byzantine Empire, established a colony called "Pera" in Galata, north of the Golden Horn, and gradually expanded their sphere of control with permissions granted by the Byzantines.

Known at the time as the "Tower of the Holy Cross" (Turris Sancte Crucis) because of the cross at its summit, the tower was built between 1335 and 1349 as part of the fortifications constructed in the area, after the Genoese expanded their sphere of control toward the hill to the northeast in violation of these permissions.
The war that broke out between the two states that year ended with a treaty signed the following year, and the hill on which the tower stood was placed under Genoese control.
Following the conquest of Constantinople by the Ottoman Empire on 29 May 1453, the Genoese in Pera surrendered the colony to the Ottomans without resistance.

Although some damage was inflicted on the fortifications in Galata, including the tower, destruction of the tower was halted by decree of Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II, and the damaged sections were rebuilt. The tower, which was damaged in the earthquake of 1509, was repaired by 1510.

In the 16th and 17th centuries, it was used to house prisoners of war and as a supply warehouse, from the 18th century onward, it was used as a fire lookout tower by the Mehterhane corps and fire watchers.
Following the fire of 1794, repairs altered the tower's design, and its upper section was converted into a coffeehouse. Its design was changed once again after the fire of 1831.
After its roof collapsed during a storm in 1875, two timber-framed masonry floors were added above the top floor, and this section began to be used to observe and report fires in the city.

During restoration work between 1965 and 1967, the tower was arranged as a tourist attraction with floors serving different purposes, and its roof was renewed in a style resembling its design between 1832 and 1876.

During this period, it was leased from the Istanbul Municipality and operated by Ünal Kardeşler and, subsequently, by a company belonging to their heirs. Its exterior underwent restoration in 1999, 2000. In 2013, BELTUR, affiliated with the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, took over its operation.

At that time, the top two floors housed a café and a restaurant, respectively. That same year, it was included on UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage Sites. In 2019, ownership and operation passed to the Directorate General of Foundations.
Following work carried out in 2020, the tower was converted into a museum and exhibition venue. Restoration work was undertaken on its roof in 2023.
59 m tall to the tip of its roof. Its cylindrical shaft is made of stone. It has 11 floors, including a basement, a ground floor, and a mezzanine.

An elevator runs from the ground floor to the sixth floor, while stone stairs extend from the ground floor to the fourth floor and steel-structure stairs from the sixth to the eighth floor. The conical roof covering the summit is made of reinforced concrete.
Today, the ground floor serves as a ticket-control and security area, and the entrance to the elevator reaching the sixth floor is also located there. The first floor houses the museum shop.

The next three floors contain permanent museum and exhibition areas featuring, respectively, a simulation area with a screen showing an animation of Hezârfen Ahmed Çelebi gliding from the Galata Tower, exhibits concerning the period when the tower was used by Taqi al-Din, photographs from the Turkish War of Independence, information and artifacts relating to the Galata Tower and its walls, and exhibits about the Galata Tower and Istanbul.

Beyond the sixth floor, which serves as a transitional area, the seventh floor is a temporary exhibition space containing a scale model depicting part of Istanbul and viewing telescopes positioned by the windows. The eighth floor is arranged as an observation terrace.
The tower's exterior and the surrounding area are also used on certain special and designated days for awareness campaigns, commemorations, and celebrations.
History
Background, construction, and the Genoese period
In 1267, the Genoese, who were allied with the Byzantine Empire, established a colony called "Pera" in Galata, north of the Golden Horn.

The Genoese expanded their sphere of control toward the hill northeast of the area without authorization and, between 1335 and 1349, built fortification walls and towers surrounded by moats on the slopes of the hill. The structure now known as the Galata Tower was built in 1348.
In addition to serving as a watchtower, it was the principal tower of the fortifications intended to protect the colony's coastal section on the flat ground against a possible land-based siege.
In front of the tower stood a barbican that projected in a semicircle from the straight line of the walls and was attached to the structure on both sides.

This area, where four lines of walls converged and the main entrance to Pera was located, was the last fortification built before Pera came under the control of the Ottoman Empire. According to the plaque there, its construction was completed on 1 April 1452. During this period, the tower was known as "Turris S.
Crucis" ("Tower of the Holy Cross"), after the cross at its summit.
In August 1348, a war broke out between the Byzantines and the Genoese as a result of commercial disputes.

After the war ended in 1349 with a Byzantine victory, peace was established, and that same year a decree issued by Byzantine Emperor John VI transferred control of the hill on which the Galata Tower stood to the Genoese.
Ottoman period

Following the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople on 29 May 1453, the Genoese in Pera surrendered the colony to Ottoman control without resistance. During this period, the damage inflicted on the tower's summit was halted following an edict issued by Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II concerning Pera.
As part of restoration work led by Zağanos Pasha, the tower was raised again, and the cross at its summit was replaced with the Flag of the Ottoman Empire.

The earthquake of 1509 caused damage to the fortifications in Galata, including the Galata Tower. Repairs led by Mimar Hayreddin were completed in mid-1510, and the tower was raised again. 17 m (the beginning of the third floor), are considered evidence of repairs made after this earthquake. Sources differ regarding the extent of these repairs.
In the 16th century, the Galata Tower and the other towers along the Walls of Galata were used as accommodation and a dungeon for Christian prisoners of war working at the shipyards in Kasımpaşa.

In his 17th-century work Seyahatnâme, Evliya Çelebi wrote that the tower had formerly served as a dungeon and, in his time, as a supply warehouse for the shipyard. Taqi al-Din also carried out some work in the tower before the construction of his observatory.
From the 18th century onward, the tower was used as a fire lookout tower by the Mehterhane corps and fire watchers.

Due to damage caused by a fire on 27 July 1794, the tower was shortened and its design altered. As part of the work, rooms projecting from each side of the uppermost floor, corridors, and a reception hall were added, and this section was converted into a coffeehouse.

A large drum was installed to announce fires, while the attic was used as a dovecote. A fire on 2, 3 August 1831 caused further damage. The upper section was repaired according to an earlier design, giving the tower its present-day appearance, apart from the roof that would collapse in the storm of 1875.
